extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists, and students of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative criteria for composing and judging tragic drama (plot, character, recognition, structure, and theatrical means) according to classical dramatic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as complete action producing pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of a complete action and of events inspiring fear or pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an effect is best produced when the events come on us by surprise and when they follow as cause and effect; the tragic wonder is greater when events seem designed rather than mere coincidence (example: the statue of Mytys at Argos). Plots constructed on these principles are necessarily the best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either Simple or Complex: Simple when change of fortune occurs without Reversal or Recognition; Complex when the change is accompanied by Reversal, Recognition, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex actions (with reversal/recognition) are superior when those moments arise from the internal structure of the plot so that what follows is necessitated or probable rather than gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of the Situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject to the rule of probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal must follow plausibly from preceding incidents (examples: messenger in Oedipus intending to cheer but producing opposite effect; Lynceus/Danaus story). Reversals should be internally motivated, not arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best form of recognition is coincident with a Reversal of the Situation (as in Oedipus). Although recognitions can take other forms (objects, proofs), recognition of persons linked with reversal most powerfully produces pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal and Recognition must arise from plot's internal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal and Recognition should arise from the internal structure of the plot so that ensuing effects follow by necessity or probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They must not be introduced from outside or by accident; the unravelling and complication must be generated by the plot itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of Suffering as necessary element
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily agony, wounds) and is an element of the whole tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scene of suffering should be used where appropriate as one of the parts that make up tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into Prologue, Episode, Exode, and Choric song (Parode and Stasimon); some plays also have actors' songs and Commos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Prologue precedes the Parode; Episode lies between complete choric songs; Exode has no choric song after it; Parode is the first chorus utterance; Stasimon is a choric ode without anapaests or trochaic tetrameters; Commos is a joint lamentation of Chorus and actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to excite pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should imitate actions which excite pity and fear — this is the distinctive mark of tragic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore plot and incidents must be selected and handled so as to produce these emotions rather than merely shock or moral satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate moral character of protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should not be eminently good and just nor an utter villain; rather a person 'between' extremes whose misfortune is brought about not by vice but by some error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a figure (e.g., Oedipus, Thyestes) arouses pity (by unmerited misfortune) and fear (by similarity to ourselves). Avoid virtuous man brought to adversity (moves neither pity nor fear), a bad man rising to prosperity, or the downfall of the entirely wicked (inspires moral satisfaction but not pity/fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune direction
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should be from good to bad, not from bad to good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The misfortune should result from error/frailty rather than vice; the effect is strongest when a renowned prosperous person falls through error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity/singleness of issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single in its issue rather than double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots with a single catastrophic issue are superior; double-thread plots (opposite catastrophes for good and bad) may please weaker spectators but do not produce true tragic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer internal structure over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity are best aroused by the inner structure of the piece rather than by spectacular means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot should be so constructed that even when heard without sight the tale produces horror and pity (e.g., hearing Oedipus's story). Relying on spectacle risks producing the monstrous rather than the terrible and is a less artistic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances that maximize pity/terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic actions are most effective when they occur between persons who are friends or near or dear to one another (kinship, close ties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: brother killing brother, son his father, mother her son, etc. Such ties heighten pity and terror. If an enemy kills an enemy, pity is rarely aroused except by the suffering itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful handling of traditional material
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may not destroy the framework of received legend but ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use traditional plots as sources but introduce inventive incidents and skilful arrangement to impress the tragic quality upon the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of perpetration and their dramatic ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: There are limited ways a deed of horror may be represented: done knowingly; done in ignorance; about to act with knowledge and then not act (worst); about to act in ignorance and discover before doing; best is deed done in ignorance with discovery afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking: best—perpetrated in ignorance with discovery after (startling effect without shocking); next—perpetrated outright in ignorance; worst—about to act knowing then not acting (shocking without tragic consequence). Examples: Oedipus (discovery after), Medea (knowing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: goodness (moral purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character should be good: any speech or action that manifests a moral purpose of any kind will be expressive of character; character is good if the purpose is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness here is relative to class (a woman or a slave may be 'good' within their class). Evaluate characters by the moral purpose expressed through their words and deeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: propriety (fitness to role/class/sex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character must have propriety—traits appropriate to the person's sex, class, or role (e.g., manly valour is appropriate to men but not to women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid portraits where traits are indecorous or inappropriate (examples: valour in a woman, unscrupulous cleverness when inappropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: true to life (probability/necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character must be true to life; the actions and speech of a person of a given character should follow by necessity or probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraiture should follow the rule of necessity or probability so that behavior is believable; the unravelling/complication must arise from character and plot, not arbitrary devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the subject suggested by tradition is inconsistent, the poet's portrayal must be consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid motiveless degradation or sudden incompatible transformations (examples: Menelaus in Orestes, Iphigenia's differing portrayals). Characters may be flawed but must be presented with coherent motivation throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Deus ex Machina for internal resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The unraveling of the plot must arise from the plot itself; the Deus ex Machina should be employed only for events external to the drama (antecedent or subsequent events beyond human scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use divine machine to resolve internal complications (criticised examples: Medea's resolution, Return of the Greeks in Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ennoble while preserving type
rubrics_metrics.description: Because tragedy imitates persons above the common level, the poet should reproduce the distinctive form of the original while making a likeness that is true to life and yet more beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the model of good portrait-painters: preserve the type (irascible, indolent, etc.) but ennoble it—e.g., portrayal of Achilles by Homer and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory appeals as concomitants, handled carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses are not among the essentials but are concomitants of poetry and must be treated skillfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is room for error in sensory/dramatic presentation; such means should support the plot and emotions without substituting for good structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of recognition and their artistic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition can take multiple forms—by signs/tokens (congenital or acquired), by turn of incident, invented by poet, by memory (sight/hearing), or by process of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking and notes: recognition by tokens/proof is less artistic; recognition by a turn of incident (e.g., Bath Scene) is better; poet-invented recognitions are artificial and poor; recognition by memory (sight/hearing triggers) and by reasoning are natural and artistically preferable. Examples: Odysseus's scar (tokens, can be treated skillfully), nurse/swineherd recognitions, voice/picture/musical triggers, deductive discovery (Choéphori).
